newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels and government locked in stalemate.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels and government locked in stalemate.

text.p: The Peruvian hostage crisis looked further than ever from a solution on Sunday as Marxist guerrillas holding 74 VIP hostages maintained their longest stalemate yet with President Alberto Fujimori's government.

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holding the Japanese ambassador's residence insisted they were open to dialogue, but lambasted Fujimori for "arrogance" and dug in for a long wait with their remaining captives.

The guerrillas have not released any more hostages since New Year's Day, four days ago, and Fujimori has kept his negotiator, Domingo Palermo, away from the residence since a first face-to-face meeting eight days ago.
Neither side has relaxed its uncompromising position, with the MRTA maintaining a demand for the release of some 400 jailed comrades, and Fujimori flatly refusing.

"Both the MRTA and the government through President Fujimori have shown irreconcilable positions," said opposition legislator Maximo San Roman Caceres, a former Peruvian vice president under Fujimori.
"The process of dialogue ... has become bogged down, and there is no immediate solution," he said. "It is putting at serious risk the life of many human beings."
Reflecting the growing desperation in Peru for a solution from any quarter, San Roman proposed that Pope John Paul II mediate an end to the crisis.

Another legislator has proposed that veteran crisis-broker and former U.S. President Jimmy Carter be called in, while MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa said he would accept Cuban President Fidel Castro or Russian leader Boris Yeltsin.
The only contact with the rebels was still through Red Cross officials shuttling to and fro with supplies and medicines, and occasional visits by Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani.
"We are maintaining our offer of being an intermediary of information," Red Cross spokesman Ronald Bigler told Reuters.
But he added the Red Cross could only be of limited help in reaching agreement over the main sticking points in the standoff. "Eventually it must come to face-to-face talks," he said.
Cipriani, a close friend of Fujimori's, entered the residence again on Sunday morning to celebrate Mass.

He was not acting as a formal channel of negotiation between the government and the rebels, although some commentators have suggested that he is maintaining a tenuous line of official contact with the MRTA.
Bolivian Foreign Minister Antonio Aranibar arrived in Lima early on Sunday to try and help bring about a solution.

At a news conference, Aranibar, whose country's ambassador Jorge Gumucio is among the captives, gave his backing to Fujimori's handling of the crisis and ruled out releasing four MRTA prisoners in Bolivia.

Gumucio and Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki are the only two ambassadors left in the residence. Their fellow hostages include Fujimori's brother, top Peruvian government officials and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
A Japanese newspaper reported Sunday that the MRTA rebels were demanding up to $30 million in ransom from Japanese firms whose executives they hold.

The Mainichi Shimbun, quoting "informed sources," said the MRTA had demanded the money as a "war tax." But Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was not aware of any ransom demands and that the government had not been approached.

The MRTA kept three banners displayed on the roof of the residence. They included the messages: "Nobody in here is giving up" and "Mr Fujimori, with arrogant declarations and without dialogue, there will never be a solution."
In his last public words on Thursday, Fujimori virulently rejected the rebels' claim to be fighting for Peru's poor and condemned them as "terrorists" bent on "feverish, destructive" violence.
The increasingly bitter war of words replaced signs of conciliation and dialogue before the New Year.
The stand-off began on Dec. 17 when about 20 well-armed MRTA rebels burst in to a cocktail party at the residence honouring Japanese Emperor Akihito.
In an apparent appeal to the guerrillas, Pope John Paul urged kidnappers and hostage-takers on Sunday to free their captives as a "gesture of humanity."
